{{Short description|Time during which a specific cryptographic key is authorized for use}}
A '''cryptoperiod''' is the time span during which a specific [[key (cryptography)|cryptographic key]] is authorized for use. [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST's]] guidelines<ref>[http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57Pt3r1.pdf NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 Revision5, Recommendation for Key Management], Relevant information located (NIST, 2020, pp. 45-47).</ref> typically recommend a long-term cryptoperiod of 1 - 3 years for [[Public-key_cryptography|asymmetric keys]]
<ref>https://www.keylength.com/en/4#Biblio10</ref> and ≤ 2 years for [[Symmetric-key algorithm|symmetric keys]].<ref>https://www.keylength.com/en/4#Biblio10</ref>

Factors to consider include the strength of the underlying encryption algorithm, key length, the likelihood of compromise through a security breach and the availability of mechanisms of revoking keys.

In traditional cryptographic practice, keys were changed at regular intervals, typically at the same time each day. The code word for a key change, in [[NSA]] parlance, is '''HJ''' or '''Hotel Juliet''' in the [[NATO phonetic alphabet]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://fam.state.gov/FAM/05FAH02/05FAH020520.html|title=Telecommunications Handbook|date=December 2010|publisher=U.S. Department of State Foreign Affairs|accessdate=2016-01-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://jproc.ca/crypto/terms.html|title=Common Crypto Terms}}</ref>

When cryptographic devices began to be used in large scale, those who had to update the key had to set a specific time to synchronize the re-key.  This was accomplished at the hour (H) the Julian (J) Date changed, among crypto-accountants, managers and users the jargon "HJ" became the accepted term meaning it was time to change the crypto-key.{{Citation needed|date=August 2019}}

==NESTOR in Vietnam==
During the [[Vietnam War]], the United States issued its forces a series of [[secure voice]] encryption equipment code-named [[NESTOR (encryption)|NESTOR]]. According to a U.S. Army history: "To maintain compatibility, key changes had to occur simultaneously in all units. The time chosen for this change was midnight, tactically the worst possible time because the greatest number of enemy contacts occurred from 2200 to 0200. Moreover, where several units shared the same keying device, having to move at night to change key settings was inconvenient and dangerous and added to the reasons for not using the equipment. Later the time of the daily NESTOR key change was moved to 0600."<ref>[http://www.history.army.mil/books/vietnam/divlevcom/ch08.htm Vietnam Studies—Division-Level Communications 1962-1973] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151115113450/http://www.history.army.mil/books/vietnam/divlevcom/ch08.htm |date=2015-11-15 }}, Lieutenant General Charles R. Myer, U.S. Department of the Army, 1982, Chapter 8</ref>
